h1: Cutting costs in a brewpub without hurting the beer
title: Cutting Brewpub Costs, Not Quality | Craft Beer School
desc: Where a brewpub can cut costs without changing the beer: yield, waste, utilities, stock and buying. Plus the savings that cost you customers.
teaser: Some savings are free. Others show up in the glass three weeks later. Here is how to tell them apart.
standfirst: A brewpub carries kitchen, bar, brewhouse and rent on one set of accounts. Trimming the wrong line damages the beer that brings people through the door. Here is where to look first and what to leave alone.
sections:
Before you cut anything, list the monthly costs in five groups: raw materials, utilities, staff, rent and wastage. Raw materials and wastage are usually the part the brewer controls. Rent is fixed. Utilities and staff sit in between. Our guide on cutting cost of goods without changing the beer goes deeper on the ingredients side.

The goal is to find costs that do not reach the customer's glass. Everything else is a trade-off. The trade-offs need a number before you decide.

Waste is the cheapest saving because the beer is already made. Count how much you pour away: the first pull from each line after a cleaning, trial pours, kegs left too long on tap, beer dumped because a tank sat past its date and glasses that foam over. A simple tally sheet at the bar and the cellar for two weeks shows you the pattern.

As an illustration, suppose a brewpub brews 10,000 litres a month and loses 2% to spills, dumps and line losses. That is 200 litres. At a hypothetical cost of ₹100 a litre to make, that is ₹20,000 a month. Halving the loss pays for a good draught balancing job in a few months. Use your own cost per litre, not these round numbers.
Improve yield before you cut ingredients

Extract efficiency, the share of the grain's sugar you actually get into the wort, is the most valuable number in the brewhouse. If it slips from 75% to 70%, you buy about 7% more malt for the same beer. The causes are usually small: a mill gap that drifted, a sparge that runs too fast, a grain bed that channels, a mash that sits at the wrong pH. Fix those before you consider a cheaper malt.

Do not swap specialty malts or hops for cheaper ones unless you taste the result side by side. A saving of a few paise a litre is not worth a flavour change that drives away regulars.

Cooling is often the biggest electricity load in a brewpub. Check that the glycol chiller is sized for the tanks, that tanks and lines are insulated and that nobody leaves the cold room door open on delivery days. Heating the kettle uses a lot of energy too. A gentler, shorter boil can save fuel, within limits, since a boil that is too weak leaves dimethyl sulphide in the beer. Our guides on cutting power and water in a brewpub and lower evaporation boils that save energy show where the gains are real.

Cash tied up in stock is a cost. Buy malt in the quantity you use in a few weeks rather than a year. Hops are different: they keep best frozen, so a larger order of a variety you use in every batch can make sense if you have freezer space. Ask two or three suppliers for quotes. Compare the delivered cost per kilogram including freight and the minimum order.

Watch the kitchen too. In a brewpub the food menu can carry more waste than the beer. A shorter menu with shared ingredients cuts spoilage and prep time.

• Shortening fermentation or maturation to free tank space.
  • Cutting cleaning chemical or sanitiser use below what the procedure needs.
  • Skipping water or microbiological tests.
  • Putting less yeast in, so fermentations run slow and throw off flavours.
  • Under-staffing the cellar so cleaning gets rushed.

Each of these saves a little this month. Each also raises the chance of a dumped batch or a bad pint. A single dumped 1,000 litre batch can wipe out a year of small savings.
Work it out on your own numbers

Pick one cost and one change per month. Measure for four weeks. Keep the change if the beer, the sales and the cost per litre all hold. Our guide on managing a brewpub from a second city shows how the same discipline helps when you cannot be on site. This is the kind of work Brewery Business Management is built around: costing, yield and decisions made with your own data.
faqs: What is the fastest saving in a brewpub?
Waste. Count the beer you pour away for two weeks. Spills, line losses and dumped batches are usually the cheapest to reduce because the beer is already made.
Is cheaper malt a good way to cut costs?
Rarely. Fix yield first. If you test a cheaper malt, taste it side by side with the current one before you commit.
Can I shorten fermentation to save tank time?
Not safely. Rushing leaves diacetyl and other off flavours. A better route is planning tank use so the beers are ready when you need them.
How do I know if a saving is working?
Track cost per litre, sales and a simple tasting check for four weeks. Keep the change only if all three hold.
